correctness.rationale: For all fixed degrees, reflection symmetry and the exact binomial variance identity give an isolated strict quadratic optimizer at r=2. Uniform convergence of first derivatives excludes global competitors away from the center. Odd degrees have no central atom, so strict local concavity persists. In even degrees, isolating the central mass b_n gives a smooth remainder of curvature A=b_n+1/n; the derivative quotient is r b_n δ^{r-2}-2A plus controlled errors. The exponential comparison scale proves a unique positive critical displacement for r<2 and none for r≥2. Exact stationarity yields the displacement logarithm and gain asymptotic. The standalone finite-sum script independently tests normalization and sample roots, but the infinite proof is analytic.

originality.rationale: The available main statements of Adell–Bustamante–Quesada (2015) bound generalized Bernstein absolute moments but do not give the parity-dependent maximizer bifurcation, its essential-singularity displacement, or the exponentially small gain. Berend–Kontorovich (2013) treats first absolute binomial moments and estimates, not the near-quadratic exponent. Direct semantic searches for symmetry breaking, exponent-two cusp, and an essential-singularity location gave no equivalent result. A complete 2015 full-text comparison was unavailable, so the possibility of an unobserved ancillary statement remains an originality risk rather than being represented as disproved.
residual_risks: Full text of Adell–Bustamante–Quesada (2015) remained inaccessible despite open and institutional attempts; unobserved ancillary optimization results cannot be excluded.

value.rationale: Classical Bernstein absolute moments control sharp positive-polynomial approximation errors and moment inequalities. The theorem discovers a parity-dependent change in the location of the worst parameter at the natural variance exponent two, quantifies an essential singularity invisible to any finite Taylor expansion in that exponent, and identifies the exponentially smaller sharp gain. It applies at every fixed even degree, identifies odd-degree rigidity, and is more than a selected numerical constant or routine restatement of a known moment bound.
